verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, upon Jonath-elem-rechokim [dove of silence of distant ones], of David, a miktam, when the Philistines seized him in Gath.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to the tune they call The Silent Dove Far from Home. A song of David, a miktam, set down in the day the Philistines laid hands on him in Gath.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the title the later editors placed over the psalm, and it ties the prayer to the scene of 1 Samuel 21:11–16, where David, fleeing Saul, turns up in Gath, the city of Goliath, and is recognized: 'Is this not David, the king of the land?' A man who has killed the local hero is now in the hands of the hero's countrymen. Play the fear as real; Rashi hears in the tune name David himself, a dove struck dumb far from his own land (Rashi on Psalm 56:1; compare Radak, who adds that fear drove him to feign madness).

The KJV leaves the tune name as an untranslated string, 'Jonath-elem-rechokim', and 'Michtam' likewise, so a reader never meets the image: a dove (yonah), mute (elem) or 'of silence', far away (rechokim). Whether אֵלֶם is 'silence' or, with other vowels, 'gods' is uncertain, and that is why most translations stay silent. Miktam appears in the titles of Psalms 16 and 56–60; Ibn Ezra connects it with ketem, 'fine gold' (Ibn Ezra on Psalm 56:1), but the meaning is not settled. 'Seized' (אחז) is a physical word, 'to grip'; the KJV's 'took him' makes it sound polite.

philological_notes.note: A tune title: 'dove of silence of the distant' or 'mute dove of far-off places'. Commentators read it either as a musical instrument or melody (Ibn Ezra, Meiri) or as David's self-description, a dove struck dumb among strangers (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat David).
'When [they] gripped him', from the verb for taking hold by force; the Philistines' intent is to hold him and kill him.

verses.translation_literal: Be gracious to me, God, for man has gasped after me; all the day [one] fighting oppresses me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Be gracious to me, O God. A man has opened his mouth to swallow me whole. All day long the fighter presses, and presses, and will not let me breathe.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with a cry for grace, not for rescue; the Hebrew chanan means the favour a weaker party begs of a stronger one. The speaker is cornered: one verb of hunger (sha'af), one of war (lacham), one of squeezing (lachats), all aimed at him. Rashi and Metzudat Zion hear sha'af as swallowing, citing Jeremiah 2:24, the wild ass that 'snuffs up the wind' (Rashi on Psalm 56:2); the picture is a gaping mouth, an animal gasping at prey. The same root is used elsewhere for trampling (Amos 2:7), so it is a matter of reading.

The KJV makes the enemy conditional, 'would swallow me up', where the Hebrew is a flat perfect: he has done it, or is doing it. The KJV also 'softens' 'man' (enosh, a word that stresses frailty) into 'man' without the sting: the enemy is merely human, and that irony pays off in the refrain of verses 5 and 12. Commentators identify the man as Saul (Meiri) or Achish and his servants (Radak); the text names no one.

philological_notes.note: 'He has gasped/snapped after me'; read 'swallow' by the commentators, 'trample' elsewhere (Amos 2:7). Repeated in verse 3 as a chain of the enemy's hunger.
Man as weak, mortal; the contrast with God (Elohim) frames the whole psalm.

verses.translation_literal: My watchers have gasped [after me] all the day, for many [are] fighting me, O Height.
verses.translation_dramatic: All day my enemies gape and gasp after me; there are so many of them, so many, fighting against me. O Most High, look down!
verses.directors_commentary: The single enemy of verse 2 becomes a crowd. 'Shorrai' is a rare word, from a root meaning 'to watch' (so Metzudat David: those who look at me with evil in their eyes); the KJV's 'enemies' flattens a precise image of stalking observers into a generic label. The line 'many are fighting me' ends with a single word, marom, 'height', which Rashi, Radak and Meiri take as God's title, 'O Most High' (Rashi on Psalm 56:3), so the cry is aimed upward in the same breath as the complaint; KJV 'O thou most High' follows this reading, whereas the ASV 'fight proudly' takes marom as an adverb. Ibn Ezra reads the opening as an ironic question: why should enemies gasp after me when I have many angels in the heights fighting for me? (Ibn Ezra on Psalm 56:3). That reading is his own; the text itself is not so witty.

philological_notes.note: 'My watchers/lurkers', from a root 'to look at', 'to spy'; enemies who observe in order to strike. The meaning is a gloss from the root; the form is rare.
'Height'; as a vocative, a divine title ('O Most High'), but could be adverbial 'proudly'.

verses.translation_literal: [The] day [that] I fear, I, to you I trust.
verses.translation_dramatic: And on the day the dread comes down on me, it is to You, only to You, that I lean my whole weight.
verses.directors_commentary:
Five Hebrew words, and one of them, 'ani, 'I', is grammatically unnecessary: the verb already says 'I'. Play it as a hand laid on the chest. Fear is admitted outright, with no pose of bravery, and trust is set right next to it as a choice. The speaker, in the psalm's heading, is David in Gath, hemmed in by Philistines who know who he is: a man who has just seen how fragile a refuge a foreign king's favor is. The line is the hinge of the whole psalm, repeated in refrain form in verses 5 and 11.

The KJV 'What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee' is accurate but turns a bare noun, 'day', into a clause of time, and 'trust in thee' hides the preposition. Hebrew says 'eleyka, 'toward you'. Radak ('like 'aleyka'), Ibn Ezra (comparing 'el hanna'ar hazeh hitpallalti, 'for this child I prayed', which is 1 Samuel 1:27) and Meiri (comparing 'batach el YHWH', Proverbs 3:5) all read 'el as 'al'. Yet the literal 'toward you' is the sharper image: trust here is movement, a man turning his face. Metzudat David adds that the day of greatest fear is the day he will trust, because rescue from all of them lies in God's hand.

philological_notes.note: To trust, to feel secure. The verb has the sense of throwing one's weight on something that will hold. Here it takes 'el, 'toward', where the usual construction is 'al or be-, and the commentators treat the two prepositions as interchangeable.

'I fear' in the imperfect: the fear is real but repeated and open-ended. The same verb returns negated in verses 5, 12: 'I will not fear'. The psalm moves from fear admitted to fear refused, with the same word.

verses.translation_literal: In God I praise his word; in God I have trusted, I will not fear: what will flesh do to me?
verses.translation_dramatic: In God, I will praise his word. In God I have put my trust, and I will not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the first of the psalm's refrains, and its structure is a ladder: praise, trust, no fear, then the question that dismisses the threat. The word to be praised is 'his word'. For Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David that word is God's promise through Samuel that David would be king (Radak on Psalm 56:5), so David's confidence is not a mood but the memory of a specific oath. Rashi hears something harder: even when God deals with him by strict justice, he will still praise his word.

The KJV's 'what flesh can do unto me' lets the question become a statement of fact; the Hebrew leaves it open, a rhetorical shrug. 'Flesh' (basar) is no soft word: it is the creature of skin and bone that bleeds, set against the divine. The line ends the same way in verse 12, only with 'adam', 'man', so the speaker hears himself and tightens the claim. Targum reads 'his word' as memra, the Aramaic 'Word', a common way to speak of God's active speech.

philological_notes.note: 'I praise his word'; the object is the promise, not just God himself. The same verb returns twice in verse 11, each time with 'word'.
'Flesh', mortal creature; paired with 'adam' in verse 12, as Radak observes ('the two are one').

verses.translation_literal: All the day my words they hurt; against me all their plans [are] for evil.
verses.translation_dramatic: All day long they work at my words until each one aches; and every scheme of theirs bends toward my harm.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two beats: what they do to his speech, and what they plot against his life. The verb ye'atzevu is the hard word. It comes from 'etzev, pain, grief; KJV 'wrest my words' uses an old verb meaning 'twist', which is a reasonable guess at the effect but not what the root says. The commentators read it as 'cause pain': Rashi, that his pursuers cause him pain until all his speech is sorrow and outcry; Ibn Ezra, that they grieve him because he trusts in the Name; Radak and Meiri, that they anger him; Metzudat David, that by their doing all his words become words of grief. If you want a single picture for the actors, it is the cringe of a man whose every sentence is pulled apart for evidence.

Malbim places the line in the Gath story. After David's pretended madness, the Philistines did not believe it, and tried to make King Achish resentful of David's words and bearing, so that Achish would conclude that David had come as a spy. Even after Achish sent him off, Malbim adds, their plans against him went on. The Hebrew 'all' is repeated: 'all the day', 'all their plans'. There is no moment of rest.

philological_notes.note: From 'etzev, 'pain, grief', in the intensive stem: they cause pain, they distress. KJV 'wrest' (twist) goes beyond the root. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri all read 'cause grief or anger'.
'Their plans', not just 'thoughts': the word is for what is devised and worked out. KJV 'thoughts' loses the deliberate scheming that Radak and Metzudat David both hear.

verses.translation_literal: They gather, they lie hidden; they, my heels they watch, as they have waited for my life.
verses.translation_dramatic: They gather together. They crouch out of sight. They are watching my heels, every step I take, as they wait, as they have waited, for my very life.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four verbs stalk across the line, each in the plural: gather, hide, watch, wait. The image is a hunting party, and 'heels' is exact: the hunter reads the footprint, and the ancient word for heel (akev) is the same root as 'track', the very thing the hunted cannot hide. Rashi pictures an ambush at the place they expect David to walk (Rashi on Psalm 56:7); Radak adds that the written form yitsPinu ('they make others lie in wait') shows a gang recruiting more watchers. The pronoun 'hemmah' ('they') is not needed and is placed with the heels: those, those very men.

The KJV's 'mark my steps' translates akev as 'steps', which loses the heel, the body part, and with it the echo of Jacob (the 'heel-grabber') and the serpent of Genesis 3:15. 'Soul' in 'wait for my soul' is nefesh, 'life, throat, self'; KJV 'soul' makes this sound pious when the threat is murder.

philological_notes.note: 'My heels', the track of a foot; the KJV 'steps' generalizes.
Qere 'they lie hidden'; the Ketiv יצפינו is causative, 'they post others in hiding', as Radak notes.
'My life, my throat, my self'; here the life they hope to take.

verses.translation_literal: Upon wickedness, deliverance for them? In anger bring down peoples, God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Shall they slip free because of their wrong? No. In your anger, O God, bring the nations down.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is among the hardest verses in the psalm; the Hebrew is clipped to the bone. 'Al aven palet lamo' has no verb: 'on wickedness, escape for them'. Radak and Metzudat David take it as a rhetorical question, 'is it right that they escape on account of their iniquity?' (Radak on Psalm 56:8), which is how the KJV and ASV punctuate it; the YLT reads it as a flat statement, and Rashi as 'to find salvation and wealth by way of evil' (Rashi on Psalm 56:8). The question reading gives the sharper drama: the actor should let the silence after it do the work.

The second half widens the scale from the local ambushers to 'peoples' (amim), the Philistines among whom David is stranded. Rashi's gloss: bring down this very nation, 'from their wisdom and from their plans' (Rashi on Psalm 56:8). The KJV's 'cast down the people' is an acceptable rendering of the imperative; 'in anger' is the same word 'af' as 'nose', the burning nostril of divine rage.

philological_notes.note: 'Deliverance, escape', a noun-like infinitive; Rashi takes it as 'to be delivered'. The verse has no verb and no question word.
'Wickedness, trouble'; a word for harm done with mischief.

verses.translation_literal: My wandering you yourself have counted; put my tears in your skin-bottle: [are they] not in your scroll?
verses.translation_dramatic: My wanderings, You have counted every one. Take my tears and keep them in Your own wineskin. Are they not already written in Your book?
verses.directors_commentary:
The most tender verse of the psalm, and its images are small and domestic. A no'd is a skin bag, the ordinary container for water or milk (Metzudat Zion compares the milk-skin of Judges 4). A tear is a drop, and a skin is made to be filled drop by drop. Radak reads the image as a way of saying 'keep them and do not forget'; Ibn Ezra, that not one drop is lost.

Two plays on sound and sense are hidden here. The first is noted by Ibn Ezra and Meiri: nodi, 'my wandering', and no'dekha, 'your skin-bottle', sound almost the same, so that David's restless wandering is poured into God's container. The second I notice for myself: the root ספר occurs twice, as safarta ('you have counted') and sifratekha ('in your scroll'). One root means both counting and writing down, so God both numbers the moves and records the tears. KJV 'thou tellest my wanderings' uses 'tell' in its old sense, 'count', which modern readers miss entirely, and 'book' for sifra is correct but loses the sense of a ledger. Rashi says the counting is of the places to which David fled, and takes sifra as an account in which the tears are reckoned together with his other troubles. (He adds that Menachem takes the word to mean a real book.) Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri take both pictures as figures of speech: the tears are kept, as a thing written in a book is kept. Malbim goes furthest: the tears are to be added to God's sum of wanderings, so that the time of exile shrinks in proportion to the grief.

Stage the second half of the verse as a question that expects 'yes'. Meiri notes that halo, 'is it not', is a word of emphasis, as in Joshua 1:9 and Ruth 2:8.

philological_notes.note: 'My wandering', a noun from the root for roaming; Ibn Ezra takes it as a short form of nedudai, and compares 'he dwelt in the land of Nod' (Genesis 4:16, so also Meiri). The pun with no'dekha, 'your skin-bottle', is noted by both Ibn Ezra and Meiri.
The same root twice: counting, then a written record. Hebrew uses one family of words for numbering and for writing. My own observation; the commentators take each word separately.
A skin bottle for water or milk, the ordinary vessel of a wandering household. Metzudat Zion cites the milk-skin of Judges 4.

verses.translation_literal: Then my enemies will turn back, backward, on the day I call; this I know, that God [is] for me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then they will turn, my enemies, they will fall back, on the day I call. This I know: God is for me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood changes here from complaint to certainty. 'Then' (az) follows the picture of the tears in God's wineskin: the enemy retreats when the prayer is made. The enemies turn 'backward' (achor), the posture of a defeated force, shoulders to the rear. Ibn Ezra and Radak take the logic as cause and effect: when I call and they see them retreat, then I know God is on my side (Radak on Psalm 56:10). Malbim ties it to the Gath episode, the Philistines who followed David turned back after his prayer (Malbim on Psalm 56:10) — a reading of his own.

'Zeh yada'ti' ('this I know') is stark: 'this' is the sign, the retreat. The last words, 'Elohim li', are three syllables, 'God [is] for me', a bare statement. The KJV adds 'unto thee' ('when I cry unto thee'); the Hebrew has only 'on the day I call', with no stated addressee.

philological_notes.note: 'This I know', or 'by this I know' (Ibn Ezra, Radak): the retreat of the enemy is the proof.
'God [is] for me' (or 'mine'); a verbless clause with a dative of advantage.

verses.translation_literal: In God I praise a word; in YHWH I praise a word.
verses.translation_dramatic: In God, I will praise the word. In the LORD, I will praise the word.
verses.directors_commentary:
The refrain returns with a variation, and the actor must feel the second half as a sharpening. The Hebrew has no 'his': 'a word', the bare noun, as if the word were so familiar that it needs no owner. The only change is the divine name: 'Elohim' in the first half, 'YHWH' in the second. The rabbis heard in this a pairing of two attributes, God as judge (Elohim) and God as merciful (YHWH). So Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat David: whether he deals with me by justice or by mercy, I will praise (Rashi on Psalm 56:11, citing Yerushalmi Berakhot 9:5). Targum has the same pairing.

The KJV supplies 'his word' in both halves and writes 'the Lord' for YHWH, hiding both the name change and the bare noun. Here the literal layer keeps YHWH. Psalms 42–83 are the Elohistic Psalter, where YHWH is mostly replaced by Elohim; YHWH standing here in the midst of Elohim is therefore conspicuous, and may be a deliberate step into the personal name (my reading).

philological_notes.note: God as 'Elohim' and as YHWH side by side; the tradition reads attribute of justice and attribute of mercy.

verses.translation_literal: In God I have trusted, I will not fear: what will man do to me?
verses.translation_dramatic: In God I have put my trust. I will not be afraid. What can a man do to me?
verses.directors_commentary:
The refrain closes, and the second time the weight has shifted. In verse 5 the foe was 'flesh' (basar); now he is 'adam', man, the creature from the ground. Radak notes that the two are one (Radak on Psalm 56:12). The shift is slight but it makes the threat smaller each time it is named. The question 'what will man do to me?' is not an inquiry. It is what the actor says with a steady voice after the whole psalm of ambushers, watchers and gatherers.

The KJV's 'I will not be afraid what man can do unto me' gives the Hebrew question the grammar of a subordinate clause, so that it stops being a question. Metzudat David reads it as faith holding even under strict judgment: even when God's justice is on me, no man can do more (Metzudat David on Psalm 56:12).

philological_notes.note: 'Man', from adamah, ground; the same enemy as 'basar' in verse 5, named by his earthly origin.

verses.translation_literal: Upon me, God, [are] your vows; I will pay thank-offerings to you.
verses.translation_dramatic: What I promised You in the dark still rests on my shoulders, O God, and I will carry it to Your altar, a thank-offering laid down before You.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns from plea to payment. 'Upon me' is the language of debt: the vows lie on David like a load he has agreed to bear. In the ancient world a vow made in trouble, 'if you save me, I will offer', was a binding contract, and deliverance triggered the debt at once. Metzudat David reads it that way: the vows were made in the hour of need, and I must now pay them with thanks and praise. Ibn Ezra reports two readings: some say the vow is 'in God I have trusted'; he prefers a vow of burnt offerings.

The word toda is the point where English drifts. KJV 'praises' (Webster follows it) abstracts the word, and BBE speaks of 'offerings of praise', but a plural toda (todot) is the name of a sacrifice. Radak glosses it as zivchei toda, 'thanksgiving sacrifices', which a person offers on being saved from distress, and the Targum has qurbanei todan, 'thank-offering sacrifices'. So the picture is an animal brought to the sanctuary and a shared meal, not a hymn alone. Meiri takes a gentler line: the 'vows' are the acknowledgement and prayer due for God's wonders.

Malbim offers a different grammar. 'Your vows' would be God's own: a prophet's promise is a kind of vow, so God vowed the kingship through Samuel and the return to Judah through Gad, and David accepts the duty to pay thanks in return. Either way, 'your vows' means vows bound to God, not simply vows I took.

philological_notes.note: 'Your vows': read by Radak and Metzudat David as vows David made to God in the exile; by Malbim, as vows God made to David through the prophets, which David then accepts as a debt of gratitude.
Plural of toda, 'thanks', which is also the name of a thanksgiving sacrifice. Radak glosses zivchei toda; the Targum qurbanei todan. This is why 'thank-offerings' is more exact than 'praises'.

verses.translation_literal: For you have delivered my life from death; [have you] not [delivered] my feet from stumbling, to walk about before God in the light of the living?
verses.translation_dramatic: For you pulled my life back from the edge of death. And my feet, were they not kept from the fall? So that I may walk here before God, in the light where the living walk.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the reason for the thank-offering, and the voice should rise from debt to wonder. Two rescues are paired: nefesh from death, then the feet from stumbling. In the ancient world, to be near death was to descend toward the dark of Sheol; the 'light of the living' is simply the daylight world, and to walk 'before God' is to live in his presence, at the sanctuary or under his eye. Light and life are one idea, so the closing phrase is an image of ordinary breathing as grace.

The KJV rewrites the second clause as a prayer, 'wilt not thou deliver my feet from falling', which makes the speaker still afraid. The Hebrew has no second verb at all; הֲלֹא is the emphatic 'Have you not…?', so the speaker is pointing to a second rescue already given and arguing from it (Radak reads the word as one of strength). Likewise לְהִתְהַלֵּךְ is the reflexive 'to walk about, to go to and fro', a habitual way of life, not a single stroll, and 'soul' is a poor modern word for nefesh, which here is simply the life, the throat that breathes. The plural 'living' is kept: the light belongs to everyone still alive.

philological_notes.note: 'My life', 'my self', the breathing person; KJV 'soul' leans toward a later, Greek sense. The parallel with 'feet' shows it is the whole bodily self that is rescued.
Hithpael infinitive: 'to walk about, to go to and fro', habitual conduct in God's presence, not a single walk.

'In the light of the living': the realm of the living, as opposed to Sheol. The tradition reads it further: Rashi takes it as return to the Land of Israel, Meiri's midrash as Eden, Metzudat David as Torah and commandments.
